routes.description: Establish that evaluative and moral concepts arise from factual requirements faced by living, choosing human beings, and that those requirements support objective guidance for flourishing and social conduct.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it identifies life-relevant facts as the referents and standard of evaluation, explains how those facts guide volitional human action, and derives non-arbitrary principles for individual and interpersonal conduct.

motionBridge.description: Connect the factual requirements of human life to truth-apt standards governing choices, actions, and character.

centralBridges.description: Explain why living organisms' conditional requirements create the factual basis and practical need for evaluative concepts.
Show how a human choice to live makes facts about survival and flourishing action-guiding without treating value as an intrinsic property.
Derive rights and constraints on force from human rational agency and each person's need to act on independent judgment.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish emotions accompanying evaluation from the cognitive identification of life-supporting or life-destructive facts.
Apply the life-based standard consistently across immortality, psychopath, animal-treatment, and consent cases.

routes.description: Establish that moral utterances express non-truth-apt emotional attitudes and that factual descriptions of life, agency, or flourishing do not themselves supply objective oughtness or binding interpersonal duties.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it provides a coherent emotivist account of moral language and experience while showing that the proposed life standard cannot non-circularly bridge facts to objective norms or explain its disputed applications.

motionBridge.description: Account for moral claims as emotive expressions while denying that life-related facts constitute objective moral properties or truth conditions.

centralBridges.description: Specify what moral predicates express and require the objectivist alternative to identify the alleged objective oughtness.
Show why a pre-moral choice to live or a factual description of flourishing cannot generate objective normative authority.
Test whether actor-centered life and flourishing can justify rights or condemn advantageous harm without assuming the disputed morality.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how emotive advocacy, rational inference, and useful rights conventions can function without objective moral truth.
Use immortality, atypical agents, and animal treatment to test the scope and consistency of the life-based account.

sections.title: Moral Meaning, Emotion, and Objective Reference
sections.rationale: This issue defines the motion-level disagreement over whether moral predicates report life-relevant facts or express attitudes without truth conditions, and it fixes what either side must explain about moral language and cognition.

sections.title: Life, Choice, and the Foundation of Value
sections.rationale: This issue covers the proposed dependence of value on living action and the choice to remain alive, together with the challenge that a conditional or pre-moral choice cannot establish objective value.

sections.title: From Life Facts to Oughts and Flourishing
sections.rationale: This issue tests the central inferential bridge from biological and human facts to action-guiding oughts, including whether flourishing clarifies the standard or expands it beyond survival without an objective warrant.

sections.title: Rational Egoism, Rights, and Moral Agency
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether a life-centered ethic can derive interpersonal rights and constraints on advantageous harm, and whether psychopath and abnormal-agent cases expose circularity or legitimate limits on moral concepts.

sections.title: Animals, Harm, and Practical Boundaries
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether the competing accounts consistently explain concern for suffering, condemnation of gratuitous harm, differences between human and animal status, and permissibility claims about animal use.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Emotivism treats ethical statements as expressions of non-propositional emotion rather than truth-apt reports about either objective facts or a speaker's preferences.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained opening turn presents the emotivist position associated with Alex O'Connor and contrasts it explicitly with subjectivism.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly states the con side's motion-level semantic thesis by distinguishing emotivism from truth-apt subjectivism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes the principal semantic position and an important contrast.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between emotivism and subjectivism makes the proposition and relevant scope readily recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents a definition of the speaker's adopted theory, and its categorical force fits that expository purpose.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The non-propositional account is internally coherent and explicitly separated from desire-dependent truth.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The definitional explanation is specific and adequate, though it does not yet defend the theory against serious rivals.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the con motion bridge's required account of moral claims as emotive expressions.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing interpretation is evaluated in this introductory statement of the emotivist account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly contrasts subjectivist truth conditions with ethical statements understood as expressions of emotion.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A materialist moral objectivist must identify what objective oughtness is and explain where it exists or originates if it is not an emotion.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly introduces this as his principal challenge to an objectivist and completes it before yielding the floor.

response.rationale: This constructive move states a central ontological and explanatory demand that the objectivist account must answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it sharply identifies the requested explanandum, although its spatial framing is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The demand is clear, but talk of objective goodness being somewhere spatially compresses the range of materialist accounts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: An objectivist owes an account of oughtness, but the suggestion that it must be a spatial object slightly overstates that burden.

charity.alternative: Objective oughtness could be a natural relation or property rather than a separately located object.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objectivist still owes an account of that relation and its normative authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The central demand is valid, but the material-object framing leaves a material ambiguity about natural relations and properties.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual challenge is supported by a stated materialist constraint, while the spatial inference remains underdefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central con requirement to specify objective oughtness and challenge its ontological basis.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge preserves the explanatory demand but its spatial language somewhat weakens the strongest naturalist alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks both what goodness is if not emotion and where it originates under a materialist ontology.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Because only living organisms pursue values to preserve their existence, life is the ultimate factual foundation of value and evaluative concepts.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle develops the life-based derivation continuously, using organisms and their goal-directed activity as the central examples.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the proposed factual basis of value by connecting goal pursuit and conditional survival to living organisms.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the foundational biological dependence clearly but compresses the normative bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The life-dependence thesis is recoverable and stable, with the conditional character of value mostly conveyed contextually.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The excerpt supports life's necessity for organismic value pursuit, but calls it the foundation of all evaluation with limited rival comparison.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dependence of biological goal pursuit on life is coherent, but the move leaves a material bridge to all evaluative concepts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Organismic dependence supplies relevant support, while the universal conclusion is asserted without representative rival testing.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central pro bridge identifying living requirements as the factual basis of value.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its positive foundation without expressly testing a developed alternative account of value.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that only living things pursue values and must do so conditionally to remain alive.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: For volitional human beings, oughts identify life-supporting actions, while chosen values and virtues organize the rational pursuit of continued life and flourishing.
moves.attributionBasis: The same pro turn explicitly moves from the biological basis of value to human choice, rational guidance, moral values, and virtues.

components.text: Explain what objective oughtness consists in and how it arises rather than merely naming goodness.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the demand by identifying oughts with rational guidance keyed to factual requirements of chosen human life, though it does not fully establish objective authority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that contacts the decisive explanatory demand but leaves the fact-to-authority bridge compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The action-guiding account is clear, but its dependence on choosing life is not fully qualified in this selected span.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Humans plausibly need guidance to pursue life, but calling factual requirements the moral standard outruns the supplied derivation.

charity.alternative: The con demand asks for objective normative authority, not merely useful conditional guidance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Conditional life guidance still explains part of what the pro side means by an ought.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The means-end guidance inference is coherent, while the transition from chosen ends to objective moral oughts remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The need for rational guidance is plausibly stated, but free will and factual requirements do not alone establish moral authority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro bridge from human volition and life requirements to normative guidance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the explanatory issue indirectly but does not fully confront the distinction between guidance and authority.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt connects rational guidance, factual human-life requirements, free will, and chosen moral values.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Moral objectivity consists in a cognitive relation to life-relevant facts, and evaluative concepts lose their basis when severed from the life conditions that make them necessary.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle directly addresses the outstanding concern about oughtness through Rand's subjective-intrinsic-objective trichotomy and its conceptual consequence.

components.text: Identify what objective goodness is within a materialist account and explain its source.
Address the claim that ethical statements express emotion rather than truth-apt factual cognition.

response.rationale: The reply answers both demands by construing objectivity as a mind-fact cognitive relation grounded in life conditions, although normative authority remains compressed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the central ontological and semantic demands, with one important explanatory bridge left implicit.

precisionFindings.rationale: Objectivity is expressly defined as a cognitive relation, and the relevant life-based scope is stated clearly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conceptual proposal is clear, but asserting life as the exclusive basis of evaluative terms lacks full rival comparison.

charity.alternative: The con side could accept mind-fact cognition generally while denying that moral predicates report life facts.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must establish that the relevant life relation supplies moral truth conditions rather than practical description alone.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The relational conception avoids treating value as a separate object, but it incompletely bridges factual cognition to moral objectivity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The life-dependence explanation is relevant, though the exclusivity and normative significance of that relation remain asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the con ontological demand by offering a naturalistic relational account of objectivity.

representationalCharity.rationale: It offers a serious alternative account to emotivism but does not fully address the strongest semantic qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines objective as a mind-fact connection and ties evaluative concepts to facts making value necessary.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: If immortal volitional people could still care about one another and suffer, ethics would remain applicable despite the complete absence of possible death.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly tests Biddle's stated restriction of ethics to mortal life with a developed immortality counterexample.

components.text: Show that life's mortality and preservation requirements are necessary for evaluative and ethical concepts.
Show that life-supporting guidance exhausts ethical relevance for volitional agents.

response.rationale: The hypothetical directly tests whether ethics would disappear when death is impossible while suffering and interpersonal concern remain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive necessity claim through a clear counterexample, though the hypothetical's conditions invite refinement.

precisionFindings.rationale: The stipulated immortality, continuing suffering, and interpersonal treatment conditions make the counterexample's scope explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move needs only a coherent possibility to test the necessity claim and expressly presents the scenario hypothetically.

charity.alternative: Life-based value could concern flourishing and vulnerability rather than only avoidance of death.
charity.decisiveQualification: The stipulated immortal agents still suffer and care, so some life-relevant conditions remain despite no death.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample coherently separates mortality from suffering and concern, challenging an overly narrow necessity claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: As a modal counterexample it is specifically stipulated, though it does not defeat every broader account of living flourishing.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the subsidiary pro requirement of coherent application to the immortality boundary case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The case fairly pressures a death-centered formulation while leaving room for the stronger flourishing-based account.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt stipulates people who live forever and asks whether treatment of others would thereby cease to matter.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A survival-based egoistic ethic appears unable to condemn recreational animal torture when the act neither threatens the torturer's survival nor frustrates that person's preferences.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor introduces the objection as a direct question about rational egoism and develops the animal-torture case through the end of his turn.

components.text: Explain how actor-centered life-supporting oughts condemn gratuitous animal torture that does not impair the actor's survival.
Explain the normative significance of animal life within the proposed factual foundation of value.

response.rationale: The reply directly tests the scope of rational egoism using a stipulated act that benefits neither survival nor frustrated preferences.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive application demand and isolates the apparent gap with a concrete counterexample.

precisionFindings.rationale: The recreational, non-survival-affecting case and the actor-centered target are sufficiently explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is appropriately framed as an apparent inability and a request for explanation rather than a conclusive refutation.

charity.alternative: A rational egoist may condemn cruelty through character, psychological, or broader flourishing effects.
charity.decisiveQualification: The case stipulates no survival threat but does not exclude every character-based effect on flourishing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The hypothetical cleanly exposes a potential mismatch between actor-centered survival and condemnation of gratuitous cruelty.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stipulated example supports the challenge, although broader flourishing or character warrants remain possible alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It very strongly attacks the subsidiary pro requirement of coherent treatment of animal-abuse cases.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge targets a strong simple survival account while leaving a bounded route for a richer egoist response.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly asks how survival-oriented rational egoism classifies intuitively unethical animal torture.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Gratuitous animal abuse is immoral because life supplies a standard of value beyond humans, and purposeless destruction manifests contempt for life.
moves.attributionBasis: The response follows O'Connor's animal-abuse question, and the sustained explanation is delivered by Biddle apart from brief acknowledgments.

components.text: Explain why gratuitous animal torture is wrong when it does not threaten the torturer's immediate survival.

response.rationale: The reply condemns unnecessary pain and purposeless destruction by extending life's value standard beyond humans, but it only partially derives the actor's obligation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive animal-torture demand but leaves the anti-life character judgment insufficiently connected to egoistic reasons.

precisionFindings.rationale: The condemnation is clear, but the movement between biological value, moral wrongness, and nonmoral wrongness destabilizes the key term.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The broad life standard supports concern, but contempt for life is asserted as morally decisive without the needed egoistic bridge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move shifts from life's biological value to moral condemnation without explaining why purposeless destruction harms the actor's life.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Opposition to unnecessary pain is asserted and illustrated, but the decisive moral warrant remains substantially unsupported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary hard-case bridge by applying the life standard to animal abuse.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply primarily advances its own explanation and does not materially characterize a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt opposes unnecessary animal pain and extends the standard of life from humans to animals and plants.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Appealing to contempt for life assumes the disputed value of life and therefore argues circularly against someone who does not already share that valuation.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly labels the preceding justification circular and develops the objection through the flower-kicking example despite brief interruptions.

components.text: Derive animal-abuse wrongness from contempt for life without assuming life's disputed moral value.
Establish life's status as value-giving rather than presupposing that status in its applications.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses circularity: contempt for life cannot justify life's value against someone who disputes that very valuation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the failing premise and states why the proposed application cannot supply the requested justification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alleged circular premise and the limited target of the objection are expressly and stably identified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker qualifies the diagnosis as how the reasoning seems, and the supplied premise-repetition supports that force.

charity.alternative: The pro side may offer life's conditional role as a conceptual foundation rather than intrinsic moral value.
charity.decisiveQualification: The specific animal-abuse reply still invokes contempt for life without deriving its moral significance for the actor.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnosis clearly distinguishes the disputed conclusion from a premise that merely restates its evaluative content.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The immediate wording about contempt for life provides specific support for the circularity diagnosis, with a bounded wider-account caveat.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central pro normative-guidance bridge by challenging its non-circular justificatory basis.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves the stronger conceptual-foundation possibility while accurately targeting the circularity of this application.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says the answer argues in a circle because it uses life's value to justify life's value.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Life is not intrinsically valuable; a person's choice to remain alive logically precedes evaluation and creates the need for values and action.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle marks a clarification and gives an extended first-person account of how choosing continued existence grounds the need for valuation.

components.text: Explain how life grounds valuation without presupposing that life is intrinsically morally valuable.
Explain the source and logical status of life-based oughts.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the circularity challenge by denying intrinsic value and locating valuation after a pre-evaluative choice to live, while leaving objectivity conditional.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the intrinsic-value version of circularity but does not fully answer whether the resulting norms are objective.

precisionFindings.rationale: The logical-dependence claim, denial of intrinsic value, and condition of choosing continued life are clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stipulated practical conception of value, the conditional claim that no ends are needed without choosing life is proportionate.

charity.alternative: The circularity objection concerns objective moral authority, not only whether life has intrinsic value.
charity.decisiveQualification: Denying intrinsic value answers one premise concern but leaves the authority of the pre-moral choice unresolved.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between intrinsic value and a precondition of valuation is coherent and resolves the simplest circular formulation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The practical example supports logical dependence, though it does not independently establish universal normative authority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro normative-guidance bridge by explaining the choice-dependent basis of valuation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly reframes the foundation as conditional logical dependence while preserving the strongest remaining objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies intrinsic value and uses the no-desire-to-live scenario to explain valuation's logical dependence.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A pre-moral choice to live cannot supply objective normativity, because an objective requirement to remain alive must be independently established or the resulting moral system remains conditional on a nonobjective choice.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor introduces several objections, then persistently questions whether objectivity can enter through the choice between living and dying.

components.text: Show how a pre-moral choice to live can yield objective rather than merely conditional normativity.

response.rationale: The reply directly identifies the unresolved dilemma: either remaining alive is independently objectively required or subsequent norms depend on a nonobjective choice.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive inferential gap and states both alternatives that the pro account must resolve.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditionality dilemma and the meanings of pre-moral and objective are sufficiently explicit in the exchange.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The dilemma follows from the pro side's express classification of the choice as pre-moral and pre-rational.

charity.alternative: Objective hypothetical requirements may follow once an agent chooses life without an objective duty to choose it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such requirements remain conditional and do not by themselves establish categorical authority over every agent.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument cleanly identifies the missing bridge between a pre-moral elective condition and objective moral authority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The pro side's own characterization of the choice supplies specific support, and the dilemma needs little empirical evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central con fact-norm bridge by exposing conditionality in the life-choice account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection accurately accommodates conditional objectivity and isolates the remaining motion-level limitation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks whether staying alive is objectively right after the pro side calls that choice pre-moral and pre-rational.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: The requirements of human life support universal moral principles, including individual rights, because each person's life is their own and requires action on personal judgment.
moves.attributionBasis: Biddle answers directly with the Frederick Douglass slavery example and develops the classification-based principle culminating in individual rights.

components.text: Explain how life-based principles extend beyond one chooser to universal interpersonal constraints.
Provide a non-intrinsic route from human-life requirements to moral principles.

response.rationale: The reply extends the account to shared human nature, separate lives, personal judgment, and rights, but the derivation from those facts remains compressed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the interpersonal consequence of the gap but only partially addresses the underlying objective-authority challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The universal-rights proposition is clear, though the conditions linking ownership of one's life to rights remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Separate agency is relevant to rights, but the claim that it gives rise to rights exceeds the articulated bridge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from distinct lives and judgment to enforceable individual rights leaves a material normative bridge unstated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Human separateness and agency provide relevant factual support, but the universal rights warrant is materially compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro bridge deriving rights and social principles from human-life requirements.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances a positive rights derivation without expressly examining a developed opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt moves from each person's separate life to life-derived moral principles and individual rights.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: A murderer who values his own life and genuinely benefits from killing an innocent person is a counterexample to grounding moral obligation solely in the actor's life and flourishing.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly separates the actor from the victim and constructs the hypothetical through repeated clarification after Biddle questions its realism.

components.text: Show why another person's rights constrain an actor whose own life genuinely benefits from murder.

response.rationale: The stipulated murderer directly tests whether actor-centered flourishing alone entails respect for another person's rights.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive interpersonal derivation with a focused counterexample and clear benefit stipulation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The innocent victim, genuine benefit, and actor-centered valuation are explicit, making the counterexample readily recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The hypothetical is expressly stipulated and appropriately offered as a possible counterexample to a universal derivation.

charity.alternative: Murder may generally damage an actor's character, security, or long-term flourishing even when it appears advantageous.
charity.decisiveQualification: The hypothetical stipulates genuine all-things-considered benefit, so a universal principle must handle that limiting case.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The stipulated case validly pressures any universal prohibition derived solely from the acting person's flourishing.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A conceptual counterexample can operate by stipulation, though its force is limited against independently universalized agency principles.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con interpersonal-counterexample bridge concerning advantageous harm and rights.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move anticipates ordinary empirical objections by stipulating genuine benefit and thereby targets the conceptual claim fairly.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt carefully stipulates an innocent victim and a murderer whose life and flourishing genuinely improve.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Invoking rights to constrain rational egoism presupposes the objective moral properties under dispute and does not explain why an egoist should care about another person's rights.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor directly identifies rights as the allegedly assumed premise and follows Biddle's brief denials with a focused question about their egoistic basis.

components.text: Derive another person's rights from rational egoism without presupposing the disputed moral constraint.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the rights appeal as assuming the disputed constraint and asks why an actor-centered egoist should recognize it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the alleged presupposition, its consequence for the derivation, and the unanswered egoistic demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenged premise, actor-centered framework, and requested explanation are all expressly and consistently identified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately frames its conclusion as a focused explanatory challenge supported by the preceding rights invocation.

charity.alternative: Rights may be factual recognitions of reciprocal agency requirements rather than primitive moral properties.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro side must still explain why those requirements bind a genuinely advantaged violator.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objection coherently distinguishes invoking a right from deriving why that right constrains a rational egoist.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The prior appeal to rights supplies direct support, although a fuller reciprocal-agency derivation could answer the challenge.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central con interpersonal bridge by challenging the non-question-begging derivation of rights.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection permits a derivative naturalistic account while accurately retaining the actor-centered bindingness question.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks what rights are and why an egoist focused on personal survival should care about another's rights.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Individual rights recognize the factual human need for freedom to act on rational judgment, while rights violators may forfeit freedom needed to threaten others.
moves.attributionBasis: The exchange explicitly gives Biddle the floor to define rights, and the sustained answer presents his stated Objectivist position.

components.text: Explain what rights are and why they matter within a life-based rational-egoist framework.
Explain why force and murder remain prohibited even when a violator claims personal benefit.

response.rationale: The reply defines rights as recognition of the factual need for freedom from force and connects enforcement to independent human agency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts both the definition and practical constraint, though reciprocal bindingness remains partly implicit.

precisionFindings.rationale: Rights, freedom from force, independent agency, and the treatment of violators are stated with stable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Freedom is plausibly necessary for ordinary rational life, but universal enforceable rights require an additional reciprocity warrant.

charity.alternative: The challenge is about why a benefiting violator is bound, not merely why peaceful agents need freedom.
charity.decisiveQualification: Universal protection of agency offers a response, but the move must justify applying it against every actor's claimed advantage.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The need for freedom supports rights coherently, but moving from each agent's need to universal enforcement leaves one material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The factual dependence on freedom is specifically articulated, while exceptions, reciprocity, and rival arrangements are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central pro bridge connecting rational agency, freedom from force, and individual rights.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply answers the strongest demand substantially while leaving its universalization step compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines rights through human freedom from force and the aim of independent, uncoerced agency.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Emotions register a person's values but are not instruments of knowledge; rational inquiry identifies life as the objective standard of moral value.
moves.attributionBasis: The first answer to the audience question expressly identifies Objectivism and develops its account of emotion, reason, and the standard of life.

components.text: Address the emotivist claim that moral judgments are expressions of emotion rather than cognitive knowledge.
Identify the cognitive route by which moral goodness is understood.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes emotions from cognition and identifies rational inquiry into life's requirements as the alternative epistemic route.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the semantic and epistemic issue, though it does not fully rebut noncognitivist analysis of utterances.

precisionFindings.rationale: The roles assigned to emotion and reason and the asserted life standard are clearly distinguished and recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The emotion-reason distinction is clear, but rational inquiry reaching life as the unique moral standard is underdemonstrated.

charity.alternative: Emotivism concerns the function of moral utterances and need not treat emotions as instruments of factual knowledge.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that emotions are not epistemic faculties does not by itself refute a noncognitivist semantic theory.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The positive cognitive alternative is coherent, but denying emotion as knowledge does not entail that emotivist semantics is false.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The distinction is asserted plausibly, while the inference to life as the objective standard lacks a developed warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It attacks the con motion bridge directly by opposing the emotive account with a cognitive life-fact account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply materially risks answering an epistemic claim that the strongest emotivist semantic account need not make.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says emotions register values but are not knowledge, then assigns moral understanding to rational inquiry.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Emotivism explains differential concern for animals through emotional resemblance and attachment more naturally than a rational-egoist derivation does.
moves.attributionBasis: O'Connor explicitly introduces the point as his response and contrasts an emotivist framework with Objectivism using developed examples.

components.text: Explain moral-pattern differences without treating rational cognition as identifying objective moral facts.
Explain differential emotional concern for animals and other living beings.

response.rationale: The reply offers emotional resemblance, attachment, and taboo formation as explanations for variable moral concern and contrasts them with rationalist derivation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the practical explanatory challenge with examples, though it does not fully answer the epistemic objection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative explanation is clear, but the move shifts from animal resemblance to incest taboo without fully fixing scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents emotivism as making better sense of patterns, and the cautious comparative force fits the examples.

charity.alternative: A rationalist may explain animal distinctions and taboos through harms, agency, kinship, or social consequences.
charity.decisiveQualification: Emotional regularities explain attitudes but do not alone establish that moral claims lack truth conditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory link from resemblance and attachment to differential attitudes is coherent, with a bounded semantic gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete patterns support plausibility, but representative evidence and comparison with rationalist alternatives are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary con bridge explaining emotivism's practical coherence and boundary judgments.

representationalCharity.rationale: The examples fairly pressure rationalist explanations, while the move only partly addresses their strongest possible qualifications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses differential animal concern and widespread incest taboos as patterns emotivism purports to explain.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: Human life as the standard of value means flourishing through the full exercise of human capacities, not mere biological survival, and is more fundamental than happiness.
moves.attributionBasis: The question is directed to Craig and invokes Rand; the answer expressly states Rand's position and Biddle's agreement with it.

components.text: Clarify the content of the life standard whose action-guiding and objective status is disputed.
Explain whether the standard concerns mere avoidance of death or richer human functioning.
Specify flourishing rather than immediate survival as the relevant actor-centered standard.

response.rationale: The reply clarifies that human life means full-capacity flourishing rather than bare survival, contacting several scope objections without resolving objective authority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully clarifies the intended standard but only partially answers the decisive normative and interpersonal objections.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast with mere survival and the reference to full human capacities make the intended scope explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The definitional clarification is well supported, but equating flourishing with the full life standard leaves its content underdeveloped.

charity.alternative: The objections target normative authority and concern for others, not merely a bare-survival interpretation.
charity.decisiveQualification: A richer flourishing standard answers scope compression but does not itself establish authority or interpersonal duties.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The clarification coherently broadens life to full human functioning, though flourishing's substantive criteria remain compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stated conceptual interpretation supports the clarification, but no independent warrant establishes it as the moral standard.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central pro normative-guidance bridge by specifying the end that life-based oughts guide.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly corrects a narrow reading while leaving the strongest independent objections intact.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly rejects mere survival and identifies human life with flourishing through full human capacities.

moves.speaker: Alex O'Connor
moves.proposition: Human life or flourishing does not adequately define moral goodness because it omits familiar ethical concern for other people and animals.
moves.attributionBasis: The question asks Alex what evidence would persuade him, and his sustained answer identifies definitional and existential requirements before applying them to rational egoism.

components.text: Show that human flourishing adequately captures the meaning and domain of moral goodness.
Show that the proposed definition captures familiar concern for other persons.
Show that the definition captures familiar moral concern for animals.

response.rationale: The reply directly rejects flourishing as semantically adequate and identifies omitted interpersonal and animal concerns as the decisive mismatch.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the proposed definition and gives concrete domains that the speaker says it fails to capture.

precisionFindings.rationale: The semantic target and the allegedly omitted domains of other people and animals are clearly identified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker appropriately presents a considered semantic judgment, though appeal to familiar usage does not conclusively settle meaning.

charity.alternative: A flourishing theory may include relationships, benevolence, rights, and treatment of animals within human flourishing.
charity.decisiveQualification: The theory must derive those inclusions rather than merely append them to an actor-centered standard.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The mismatch objection coherently distinguishes accepting a term's definition from accepting its adequacy for moral discourse.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Familiar concern for people and animals gives relevant examples, but broad linguistic and theoretical comparison is limited.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central con semantic account by challenging flourishing as moral truth conditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection recognizes the proposed referent but fairly presses whether its richer implications are genuinely derived.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts the proposed terms yet denies that human life or flourishing captures what moral discourse concerns.

moves.speaker: Craig Biddle
moves.proposition: General biological values differ from moral values, which arise within the sphere of human choice; valuing animal life therefore does not entail granting animals human rights.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig directly answers the audience member's follow-up and continues the same account of values, morality, rights, and animals.

components.text: Explain animal-value boundaries through principled distinctions rather than emotional resemblance alone.
Clarify why valuing animal life does not entail treating animals as human moral agents or rights holders.
Address the claimed omission of animals from the life-based account.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes biological value from chosen human moral value and uses agency to deny animals human rights, though treatment duties remain incomplete.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the boundary and rights questions but only partially answers the separate wrongness-of-cruelty demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: Biological value, moral value, human choice, and animal rights are expressly distinguished with stable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The agency distinction supports different status, but the categorical denial of rights lacks a complete account of all possible rights.

charity.alternative: Animals might lack human rational agency yet possess limited rights grounded in sentience or interests.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move establishes a difference from human moral agency but does not independently exclude every nonhuman-rights basis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The biological-moral distinction is coherent, while the inference from nonhuman agency to no rights leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Human choice supports the classification difference, but the blanket rights conclusion lacks serious alternative comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary pro hard-case bridge by distinguishing animal value from human moral rights.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly identifies a relevant agency difference but underhandles the strongest limited-rights alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes general biological values from chosen human moral values and concludes that animals lack rights.
